_HOW_TO_USE_THIS_TEMPLATE: This file is a TEMPLATE. It is not published, because its name begins with an
underscore and the build script skips such files.
TO ADD A LITERARY TEXT:
1. Copy this file and give the copy a normal name, for example:
_src/pages/ol-literature/texts/twilight-of-a-crane.json
(Create the folders if they do not exist. Do NOT start the name with _ .)
2. Change the "slug" to the address you want, for example:
ol-literature/texts/twilight-of-a-crane
3. Fill in the fifteen sections below. Delete any section you genuinely
cannot complete yet - an empty section is better than an invented one.
4. Add a short entry for the text in data/literature.json so that it appears
in the genre listings and in site search. The 'slug' there must match the
'slug' here.
5. Run build.cmd.
COPYRIGHT - READ THIS EVERY TIME:
* Do NOT reproduce the complete poem, story, play or novel, or a large part
of it, unless it is out of copyright or you have written permission.
* Quotations must be SHORT, ACCURATE and used for study and criticism, with
the author and work named.
* NEVER invent a quotation, a plot detail, a date, or a fact about an author.
If you are not certain, check the book before you publish it.
* Summaries, analysis, themes, character notes, questions and model answers
that you write yourself are your own work and may be published freely.
The fifteen sections are already laid out below in the correct order. Keeping
the same order on every text page is the whole point: a student who has used
one text page then knows where to look on all the others.
title: Title of the Text
metaTitle: Title of the Text | O/L Literature study guide | RCF English
description: Summary, characters, themes, techniques, quotations, context questions, essay questions and model answers for [title] at O/L English Literature.
keywords: title, author, O/L Literature, summary, themes, characters, model answers

hero.text: One or two sentences saying what kind of text this is and what a student should watch for while reading it.

blocks.title: About this study guide
bullets: The complete text is **not** reproduced here. You will need your prescribed book.
Quotations are short and are used for study and criticism.
The summary, analysis, questions and model answers on this page were written by RCF English.
If you find anything here that does not match your copy of the text, please [report it](corrections/).

blocks.heading: 1. Introduction
text: What kind of text this is, and where it sits in the course.
What a student should watch for as they read. Two or three sentences is enough.

blocks.heading: 2. Author or playwright
text: Who wrote it. **Verified facts only.** If you are not certain of a date, a place or a detail of a life, leave it out rather than guess.
Two or three sentences. A student does not need a biography; they need whatever helps them read the text.

blocks.heading: 3. Background
text: When and where it was written, and anything a reader needs to know in order to make sense of it - a historical situation, a social custom, a literary convention.
Only what is needed. Background that does not help the reading is background that gets memorised instead of the text.

blocks.heading: 4. Summary or plot
text: What happens, in order, without interpretation mixed in. Keep analysis for the later sections.

blocks.heading: 5. Characters
intro: Who each character is, what they want, how they change, and how they relate to the others. Prove each quality with an action rather than asserting it with an adjective.

items.definition: Who they are and what they want.
items.example: How they change, and the moment that changes them.

items.definition: Who they are and what they want.
items.example: How they change, and the moment that changes them.

blocks.heading: 6. Themes
text: State each theme as a **full sentence that could be disagreed with**, not as a single word. *Poverty* is a topic; *the story shows how poverty narrows the choices of people who are otherwise capable* is a theme.
For each theme, list three moments in the text that carry it - early, middle and late - so that development can be argued.

blocks.heading: 7. Literary or dramatic techniques
intro: Name the technique, point to where it occurs, and say what it **does**. The third part is where the marks are.

items.definition: Where it occurs in this text.
items.example: What it does to the reader or audience, and why the writer wanted that effect there.

items.definition: Where it occurs in this text.
items.example: What it does to the reader or audience, and why the writer wanted that effect there.

blocks.heading: 8. Important quotations
blocks.caption: Ten short quotations, each chosen because it is useful for more than one question. Copy them exactly from the text - never from memory.

blocks.heading: 9. Context questions
intro: Short questions on a printed extract, of the kind the paper asks. Keep every question that belongs to this text on this page.

a: Quote the short extract here (keeping within fair quotation), then the questions:
bullets: Who is speaking, and to whom?
What does the underlined phrase suggest?
What does this reveal about the speaker?

blocks.heading: 10. Concise context answers
intro: Model answers of the **right length**. Context answers should be short - one mark, one sentence.

items.label: Extract 1, answers
notes: Each answer matches the marks available.
Quotations are taken from the printed extract, exactly.
Nothing is retold that the examiner already knows.

blocks.heading: 11. Essay questions
text: Full questions on this text, of the kind the paper sets. Include some that quote an opinion and ask how far the student agrees.

blocks.heading: 12. Developed model answers
intro: A full essay answer, with notes explaining how it is built. Do not encourage memorisation - say so on the page.

items.label: Model essay answer
sample: Introduction: takes a position, and qualifies it.
Body paragraph one: point, evidence, explanation, effect, link.
Body paragraph two: a different point, not the first restated.
Body paragraph three: the complication, or the opposing view answered.
Conclusion: a judgement, not a summary.
notes: Point out where the evidence appears and how short it is.
Point out the sentence that states the effect on the reader.
Point out where the essay meets an objection.
Point out that the conclusion decides something the introduction did not.

blocks.heading: 13. Common student mistakes
text: The errors students actually make **on this particular text** - not general advice, which is already on [Common Student Mistakes](ol-literature/common-mistakes/).
bullets: A misreading that recurs every year, and the correction.
A detail students consistently get wrong, and the correct detail.
A character students misjudge, and the evidence that corrects it.

blocks.heading: 14. Revision exercises
text: Activities that require the student to produce something, rather than to reread.
numbered: Reduce this text to one side of paper: one line per scene or chapter, characters in three words each, themes as full sentences.
Write your ten quotations and, beside each, the two different questions it could answer.
Take a one-sentence answer and rewrite it as five sentences: point, evidence, explanation, effect, link.
Read the opening and the ending one after the other and write a paragraph on what has changed.

blocks.heading: 15. Related past-paper questions
text: Where this text has been examined before, so students can see the range of questions asked. Link to the [Past Papers centre](past-papers/ol-literature/) rather than copying papers here.
